# A cross-reference that points at its own entry

"Cats, see Cats" tells a reader nothing and, in HTML, links an entry to itself.
Such a target is reported and dropped; the term is then indexed as usual, which
is the one outcome that neither leaves useless output nor loses the term.

Four shapes, so that no single one stands in for the family:

A single-level `see=` naming its own `entry=`: [cats]{.index entry="Cats"
see="Cats"}.

A `see-also=` naming its own two-level `entry=` path: [owls]{.index
entry="Birds!Owls" see-also="Birds!Owls"}.

A self-target on a mark whose entry comes from its visible text rather than
from `entry=`: [ferrets]{.index see="ferrets"}.

A mark carrying both attributes, of which only the `see=` is self-targeting —
the surviving `see-also=` must still be emitted, and the both-attributes report
must still fire: [dogs]{.index entry="Dogs" see="Dogs" see-also="Pets"}.

# A cross-reference that does not

A target naming a different entry is untouched, and is what tells a
self-reference check from a check that drops every target:
[lynxes]{.index entry="Lynxes" see="Cats"}.
